newsitem.title: USA: U.S. wants resolution of Japan air cargo dispute.
newsitem.headline: U.S. wants resolution of Japan air cargo dispute.

text.p: The United States wants to resolve a long standing dispute with Japan over aviation service quickly or it might move to impose sanctions, a U.S. official said on Thursday.

Assistant Transportation Secretary Charles Hunnicutt told a Senate panel that Transportation Secretary Rodney Slater will discuss the aviation dispute with his Japanese counterpart on Monday in Canada during the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation transportation ministers meeting.

The United States wants to restart talks with Japan on an "open skies" agreement to eliminate government restrictions on aviation service. Hunnicutt said talks will also cover a long-standing dispute over Japan's refusal to approve new Federal Express Corp service routes.

"We will again make clear that the cargo services problem created by Japan needs to be resolved quickly, in the context of our broader issues," Hunnicutt told the panel. "But if not, it will be dealt with quickly on its own."
Hunnicutt told reporters sanctions were possible.

"We have an outstanding order which could be implemented for the Japanese denial for U.S. beyond rights," he said. "That is certainly within the realm of possibility. It depends on how the negotiations are going."
Last July the the United States threatened to curb cargo operations by Japan Airlines Co Ltd unless Tokyo approved flights by Federal Express between Japan and other lucrative Asian markets.

Talks to resolve the dispute broke down in August and informal discussions resumed in January. Hunnicutt said another round of informal discussions at the assistant secretary level will be held in July.

Japan has resisted U.S. calls for an open skies agreement and has instead proposed allowing two carriers broad access to each others markets. Hunnicutt said that proposal serves Tokyo's interests well because the Japanese industry basically consists of two air carriers. But the proposal would leave out a number of U.S. carriers.
U.S. officials have said they are open to discussions about an interim arrangement that would lead to a full open skies arrangement.
"The United States continues to seek a fully liberalized open skies civil aviation regime with Japan in a reasonable time frame," Hunnicut said.
